reminder: An essential [ideal](c:ideal) has a nonzero intersection with every nonzero ideal of the ring.
definition: A two-sided [ideal](c:ideal) $I$ of a [ring](c:ring) $R$ is essential when $I\cap J\neq 0$ for every nonzero ideal $J$ of $R$. In other words, $I$ is an essential [submodule](c:submodule) of $R$ in the category of bimodules: no nonzero sub-bimodule of $R$ meets $I$ only in $0$.
examples: For $n\neq 0$, the ideal $n\mathbb{Z}$ of $\mathbb{Z}$ is essential, because $n\mathbb{Z}\cap m\mathbb{Z}=\operatorname{lcm}(n,m)\mathbb{Z}$ is nonzero for every $m\neq 0$.
An ideal $I$ of a C*-algebra $A$ is essential exactly when $aI=0$ implies $a=0$; then $A$ embeds in the [multiplier algebra](c:multiplier-algebra) of $I$.
Non-example: in $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ the ideal $\mathbb{Z}\times 0$ is not essential, because it meets the nonzero ideal $0\times\mathbb{Z}$ only in $0$.

steps: Start with an [ideal](c:ideal) $I$ of the ring $R$.
Add the condition that $I\cap J\neq 0$ for every nonzero ideal $J$ of $R$.
An ideal that meets this condition is an essential ideal.
links.why: It shows what essential adds to an ideal: no nonzero ideal can avoid it.

reminder: An excircle of a [triangle](c:triangle) touches one side and the extensions of the other two sides.
definition: An excircle of a [triangle](c:triangle) $ABC$ is a [circle](c:circle) outside the triangle that is tangent to one side and to the extensions of the other two sides. Each triangle has three excircles, one opposite each vertex. The center of the excircle opposite $A$ is the point where the internal [angle bisector](c:angle-bisector) at $A$ meets the external bisectors at $B$ and $C$.
examples: In a triangle with sides $a,b,c$, area $\Delta$ and semiperimeter $s$, the excircle that touches the side $a$ has radius $r_a=\Delta/(s-a)$.
An equilateral triangle with side $1$ has three equal excircles of radius $\sqrt3/2$.
Non-example: the [incircle](c:incircle) lies inside the triangle and touches all three sides, so it is not an excircle.

reminder: The exit path category of a [stratified space](c:stratified-space) records the paths that only move from a stratum into bigger strata.
definition: Let $X$ be a [stratified space](c:stratified-space) whose strata are indexed by a [partial order](c:partial-order) $P$, where $p\le q$ when the stratum $X_p$ lies in the closure of $X_q$. The exit path (∞,1)-category $\operatorname{Exit}(X)$ is an [(∞,1)-category](c:infinity-1-category) whose objects are the points of $X$. Its morphisms are the exit paths, which are paths whose stratum can only grow as time runs.
examples: For $X=[0,1)$ with the strata $\{0\}$ and $(0,1)$, the category $\operatorname{Exit}(X)$ is equivalent to the category with two objects and one arrow $0\to 1$.
If $X$ has a single stratum, every path is an exit path, and $\operatorname{Exit}(X)$ is the [fundamental infinity-groupoid](c:fundamental-infinity-groupoid) of $X$.
Non-example: the reverse of an exit path that leaves the stratum $\{0\}$ is not an exit path, because it moves from the bigger stratum back into the smaller one.

steps: Take a space $X$ with only one stratum.
Then every path is an exit path, because the stratum never changes.
So every morphism of $\operatorname{Exit}(X)$ is invertible up to homotopy, as in a groupoid.
This gives the [fundamental infinity-groupoid](c:fundamental-infinity-groupoid) of $X$, so the exit path category adds the strata and drops invertibility.
links.why: It shows that exit paths extend the fundamental infinity-groupoid to spaces with several strata.

reminder: For a [faithfully flat](c:faithfully-flat) map $A\to B$, an $A$-module is the same as a $B$-module with descent data.
definition: Let $A\to B$ be a [ring homomorphism](c:ring-homomorphism) such that $B$ is a [faithfully flat](c:faithfully-flat) $A$-[module](c:module). Then $M\mapsto B\otimes_A M$ is an equivalence from $A$-modules to $B$-modules $N$ with [descent data](c:descent-data), that is, an isomorphism $\varphi:N\otimes_A B\to B\otimes_A N$ of $B\otimes_A B$-modules that satisfies a cocycle condition over $B\otimes_A B\otimes_A B$. The inverse sends $N$ to the set of elements $n$ with $\varphi(n\otimes 1)=1\otimes n$.
examples: Galois descent: for a finite Galois extension $L/K$, vector spaces over $K$ correspond to $L$-vector spaces with a semilinear action of $\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$.
For faithfully flat $A\to B$ and any $A$-module $M$, the sequence $0\to M\to B\otimes_A M\to B\otimes_A B\otimes_A M$ is exact, so $M$ is rebuilt from $B\otimes_A M$.
Non-example: the map $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}$ is flat but not faithfully flat; the module $\mathbb{Z}/2$ has $\mathbb{Q}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Z}/2=0$, so it cannot be recovered.

steps: Descent asks when objects over a base can be rebuilt from objects over a cover together with gluing data.
Take as the cover the faithfully flat map $A\to B$, which is the map of affine schemes $\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A$.
Take modules as the objects, and take descent data on $B\otimes_A B$ as the gluing data.
The special case adds the result that gluing always works: modules over $A$ are exactly the modules over $B$ with descent data.
links.why: It shows which cover makes descent work for modules: a faithfully flat ring map.

reminder: The Fermat point of a [triangle](c:triangle) is the point with the smallest sum of distances to the three vertices.
definition: For a [triangle](c:triangle) $ABC$, the Fermat point is the point $P$ of the plane that minimizes $PA+PB+PC$, where $PA$ is the [distance](c:distance) from $P$ to $A$. If every [angle](c:angle) of the triangle is less than $120^\circ$, then $P$ lies inside the triangle and the segments $PA$, $PB$ and $PC$ meet in pairs at $120^\circ$. If one angle is at least $120^\circ$, then $P$ is the vertex of that angle.
examples: In an [equilateral triangle](c:equilateral-triangle) the Fermat point is the center, and it sees each side at $120^\circ$.
Construction: build an equilateral triangle outward on each side; the three lines from the new vertices to the opposite vertices meet at the Fermat point when all angles are below $120^\circ$.
Non-example: the centroid minimizes the sum of the squared distances, not the sum of the distances, so for most triangles it is not the Fermat point.

reminder: A [field extension](c:field-extension) $L/K$ has finite transcendence degree when it is algebraic over a finitely generated intermediate extension.
definition: A [field extension](c:field-extension) $L/K$ has finite [transcendence degree](c:transcendence-degree) when there is an intermediate field $E$ with $K\subseteq E\subseteq L$ such that $E/K$ is finitely generated and $L/E$ is an [algebraic extension](c:algebraic-extension). Equivalently, the transcendence degree $\operatorname{trdeg}_K L$ is a finite number.
examples: The field $K(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ of rational functions has transcendence degree $n$ over $K$, so it is finite.
Every algebraic extension, such as $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q}$, has transcendence degree $0$: take $E=K$.
Non-example: $K(x_1,x_2,\dots)$ with infinitely many variables has infinite transcendence degree over $K$, and so does $\mathbb{R}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.

steps: Let $L/K$ be an [algebraic extension](c:algebraic-extension).
Take $E=K$, which is finitely generated over $K$.
Then $L/E$ is algebraic, so $L/K$ has finite transcendence degree, namely $0$.
The general case allows $E$ to be a larger finitely generated field, which adds finitely many free parameters.
links.why: It shows that finite transcendence degree extends algebraic extensions by finitely many free parameters.

reminder: Two [fixed points](c:fixed-point) of $f$ share a class when a path between them is homotopic to its image under $f$, with ends fixed.
definition: Let $f:X\to X$ be a [continuous function](c:continuous-function). Call two [fixed points](c:fixed-point) $x$ and $y$ of $f$ equivalent when there is a path $\gamma$ from $x$ to $y$ such that $\gamma$ and $f\circ\gamma$ are [homotopic](c:homotopy) relative to the end points. This is an [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation) on the set of fixed points, and its classes are the fixed point classes.
examples: For the identity map of a path-connected space, all points are fixed and they form one fixed point class, because $f\circ\gamma=\gamma$ for every path $\gamma$.
A map with a single fixed point has exactly one fixed point class, as for $z\mapsto z^2$ on the unit circle, where only $z=1$ is fixed.

Non-example: the fixed points $1$ and $-1$ of $z\mapsto z^3$ on the circle lie in different classes, because a path of angle $\pi+2\pi k$ has an image of angle $3\pi+6\pi k$, and these paths are not homotopic.

reminder: A $G$-spectrum is a spectrum of pointed $G$-spaces, indexed by the representations of a [compact Lie group](c:compact-lie-group) $G$.
definition: Let $G$ be a [compact Lie group](c:compact-lie-group) and $U$ a [G-universe](c:g-universe), complete in the genuine case. A $G$-spectrum indexed on $U$ gives a pointed $G$-space $X(V)$ for each finite-dimensional subrepresentation $V\subseteq U$, with equivariant structure maps $S^{W-V}\wedge X(V)\to X(W)$ for $V\subseteq W$, where $S^{W-V}$ is the [representation sphere](c:representation-sphere) of the orthogonal complement of $V$ in $W$. For the trivial group this is an ordinary spectrum.
examples: The suspension spectrum of a pointed $G$-space $A$ has $X(V)=S^V\wedge A$.
For the trivial group $G$, the $G$-spectra are the ordinary spectra, such as the sphere spectrum.
[Equivariant K-theory](c:equivariant-k-theory) is represented by a $G$-spectrum $KU_G$.
Non-example: a single pointed $G$-space is not a $G$-spectrum, because a $G$-spectrum needs a space for every representation and structure maps between them.

steps: Take $G$ to be the trivial group.
The finite-dimensional representations are the spaces $\mathbb{R}^n$, and the representation sphere $S^{W-V}$ is a sphere $S^{m-n}$.
So a $G$-spectrum is a sequence of pointed spaces $X_n$ with maps $S^1\wedge X_n\to X_{n+1}$.
This is an ordinary [spectrum object](c:spectrum-object), so the $G$-case adds the group action and the indexing by representations.
links.why: It shows that equivariant stable homotopy theory contains the ordinary one as the case of the trivial group.

steps: Take the trivial universe $U=\mathbb{R}^\infty$ with the trivial $G$-action.
Its finite-dimensional subrepresentations are the spaces $\mathbb{R}^n$ with trivial action.
A $G$-spectrum indexed on $U$ is then a sequence of pointed $G$-spaces $X_n$ with $G$-maps $S^1\wedge X_n\to X_{n+1}$.
This is a [naive G-spectrum](c:naive-g-spectrum), so the genuine case adds the other representations to the indexing.
links.why: It shows how much the genuine theory adds to naive $G$-spectra: spheres for all representations.

reminder: A genetic [algorithm](c:algorithm) improves a population of candidate solutions by repeated selection, crossover and mutation.
definition: A genetic algorithm searches for an element that maximizes a fitness [function](c:function) on a set of candidate solutions, usually strings of symbols. It keeps a population of strings, and in each round it selects strings of high fitness, recombines pairs of them by crossover, and changes random symbols by mutation. The new strings form the next population, and the process stops after a fixed number of rounds or when the fitness is high enough.
examples: OneMax: maximize the number of $1$s in a bit string of length $n$; strings with many $1$s are selected and pass their $1$s on by crossover.
For a short tour in the traveling salesman problem, a candidate is a permutation of the cities, and the crossover must again give a permutation.
Holland's schema theorem estimates how often a short pattern of fixed symbols with above-average fitness survives selection, crossover and mutation.
Non-example: gradient descent follows one candidate with a derivative and has no population, selection or crossover, so it is not a genetic algorithm.

steps: An [algorithm](c:algorithm) is a finite list of rules that turns an input into an output.
Take the input to be a fitness function and a set of candidate strings.
Let the rules be selection, crossover and mutation, applied to a population in repeated rounds.
The output is the best string found, so a genetic algorithm is an algorithm with randomness inside the crossover and mutation steps.
links.why: It shows that a genetic algorithm is an ordinary algorithm with a fixed set of random steps.

reminder: The Goodwillie-Taylor tower of a functor $F$ is the tower of its universal approximations $P_nF$ by [n-excisive](c:n-excisive-infinity-1-functor) functors.
definition: Let $F$ be an [(∞,1)-functor](c:infinity-1-functor) into a [Goodwillie-differentiable](c:goodwillie-differentiable-infinity-1-category) (∞,1)-category. For each $n\ge 0$, the functor $P_nF$ is the universal [n-excisive](c:n-excisive-infinity-1-functor) functor under $F$, so $F\to P_nF$ is the best $n$-excisive approximation. The maps $P_nF\to P_{n-1}F$ form a [tower](c:tower) $\cdots\to P_2F\to P_1F\to P_0F$ under $F$, and this tower is the Taylor tower, whose layers are the fibres $D_nF$ of the maps $P_nF\to P_{n-1}F$.
examples: For the identity functor on pointed spaces, the first stage is $P_1(\mathrm{id})(X)=\Omega^\infty\Sigma^\infty X$, the free infinite loop space on $X$.
If $F$ is already $n$-excisive, then $P_kF=F$ for all $k\ge n$, and the tower does not change from stage $n$ on.
Non-example: the sequence of Taylor polynomials of a smooth function is only an analogy; its terms are polynomials, not $n$-excisive functors.

steps: A [tower](c:tower) is a sequence of objects $X_n$ with maps $X_n\to X_{n-1}$.
Work in the [(∞,1)-category of functors](c:infinity-1-category-of-infinity-1-functors) from the source category to the target category.
Take $X_n=P_nF$, with the maps $P_nF\to P_{n-1}F$ that come from the universal property.
Then the Taylor tower is a tower in this functor category, and it sits under the functor $F$.
links.why: It shows that the Taylor tower is an ordinary tower of functors, so tower tools apply to it.

reminder: The gradient flow of a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) moves each point along the direction in which the function decreases fastest.
definition:
Let $(X,g)$ be a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) and $f:X	o\mathbb{R}$ a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) with [gradient](c:gradient) $
abla f$. The gradient flow of $f$ is the [flow](c:flow-of-a-vector-field) of the [vector field](c:vector-field) $-
abla f$, up to a sign convention, so its flow lines are the curves $\gamma$ with $\gamma'(t)=-
abla f(\gamma(t))$. Along each flow line $f$ decreases, because $ rac{d}{dt}f(\gamma(t))=-|
abla f|^2\le 0$.
examples: For $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ on the plane, the flow lines are $\gamma(t)=e^{-2t}\gamma(0)$, which run to the minimum at the origin.
For the height function on the round sphere, the flow lines run along meridians from the north pole to the south pole.
Non-example: the Hamiltonian flow of $H$ on a symplectic manifold keeps $H$ constant, but a gradient flow decreases $f$, so the two flows are different.

steps: Let $V$ be a [vector field](c:vector-field) on $X$, with flow $\varphi_t$ defined by $\frac{d}{dt}\varphi_t(x)=V(\varphi_t(x))$.
Choose $V=-\nabla f$, the negative gradient of a smooth function $f$ for the metric $g$.
The flow of this particular field is the gradient flow of $f$.
So a gradient flow adds the condition that the field is minus the gradient of a function, which makes $f$ decrease along flow lines.
links.why: It shows that a gradient flow is an ordinary flow, with the extra property that a function decreases along it.

reminder: A graph complex is a [cochain complex](c:cochain-complex) that has graphs as basis elements and a differential that contracts edges.
definition: A graph complex is a [cochain complex](c:cochain-complex) whose underlying vector space has a basis of isomorphism classes of decorated [graphs](c:graph), with orientation data so that reversing the orientation changes the sign. Its [differential](c:differential) sends a graph to a signed sum of the graphs obtained by contracting one edge, or, in the dual convention, by splitting one vertex. The decorations and the allowed graphs, such as connected graphs with all vertices at least trivalent, depend on the particular complex.
examples: Kontsevich's graph complex $GC_2$ is spanned by graphs with vertices of valence at least three; in degree zero its cohomology is the Grothendieck-Teichmüller Lie algebra $\mathfrak{grt}_1$, by a theorem of Willwacher.
The Feynman transform of a modular operad is a graph complex whose graphs are decorated with operations of the operad.
Non-example: the cochain complex of one graph, with its vertices and edges as cells, is not a graph complex, because its basis is the set of cells of one graph and not a set of graphs.

steps: Take the vector space spanned by the isomorphism classes of graphs of the chosen kind, graded so that contracting an edge raises the degree by one.
Define the differential as the signed sum over all edge contractions of a graph.
Then $d^2=0$, because contracting two edges in either order gives the same graph with opposite signs.
So the result is a [cochain complex](c:cochain-complex) whose basis is a set of graphs.
links.why: It shows that a graph complex is a cochain complex whose basis and differential are given by graphs.

reminder: A graph embedding places a [graph](c:graph) on a surface so that vertices are points and edges are arcs that meet only at common ends.
definition: An embedding of a [graph](c:graph) $G$ into a [surface](c:surface) $S$ sends each vertex to a point and each edge to an arc between the images of its end vertices, so that the points are distinct and two arcs meet only at a common end vertex. Equivalently, it is an [embedding](c:embedding-of-topological-spaces) of the topological space of $G$, a one-dimensional cell complex, into $S$.
examples: The complete graph $K_4$ embeds in the plane: draw a triangle with one vertex in the middle.
The graphs $K_5$ and $K_{3,3}$ embed in the torus.
By the Ringel-Youngs theorem, $K_n$ embeds in the orientable surface of genus $\lceil (n-3)(n-4)/12\rceil$ and in no orientable surface of smaller genus.
Non-example: $K_5$ has no embedding in the plane, because every drawing of it in the plane has two edges that cross.

steps: Regard the graph $G$ as a topological space: a point for each vertex and a unit interval glued in for each edge.
An embedding of $G$ into $S$ is then an injective continuous map that is a homeomorphism onto its image.
The graph case adds that the source is a one-dimensional cell complex, so the image is a union of arcs.
links.why: It shows that a graph embedding is an embedding of topological spaces whose source is a graph.

reminder: The group of ideles of a [number field](c:number-field) is the [group of units](c:group-of-units) of its [ring of adeles](c:ring-of-adeles).
definition: For a [number field](c:number-field) $K$, the group of ideles $\mathbb{I}_K$ is the [group of units](c:group-of-units) $\mathbb{A}_K^\times$ of the [ring of adeles](c:ring-of-adeles). Concretely, an idele is a family $(x_v)$ over all places $v$ of $K$ with $x_v\in K_v^\times$, where $x_v$ is a unit of the ring of integers of $K_v$ for almost all finite $v$. This is the [restricted product](c:restricted-product) of the groups $K_v^\times$, and its [topology](c:topology) is the restricted product topology, which is finer than the subspace topology from the adeles.
examples: Every $a\in K^\times$ gives the principal idele $(a,a,a,\dots)$, and $K^\times$ is a discrete subgroup of $\mathbb{I}_K$.
For $K=\mathbb{Q}$, every idele is the product of a rational number $q\neq 0$ and an idele in $\mathbb{R}_{>0}\times\prod_p\mathbb{Z}_p^\times$.
Non-example: the family $(p)_p$ with the entry $p\in\mathbb{Q}_p^\times$ at every prime $p$ is not an idele, because $p$ is not a $p$-adic unit at infinitely many places.

steps: Take the [ring of adeles](c:ring-of-adeles) $\mathbb{A}_K$ of the number field $K$.
Every ring has a [group of units](c:group-of-units): the elements that have an inverse in the ring.
Form the group of units $\mathbb{A}_K^\times$ of the adele ring.
This group is the group of ideles, and it carries a finer topology than the subspace topology.
links.why: It shows that the ideles are the units of the adeles, with a topology chosen to make inversion continuous.

reminder: A differential relation satisfies the h-principle when every formal solution can be deformed into a true solution.
definition: A partial differential relation $R$ is a condition on the jets of sections of a fiber bundle. A formal solution is a [section](c:section) of the [jet bundle](c:jet-bundle) that lies in $R$, whether or not it comes from a section of the bundle. The relation satisfies the h-principle when every formal solution is [homotopic](c:homotopy), through formal solutions, to the jet of a genuine solution of the [partial differential equation](c:partial-differential-equation).
examples: Smale-Hirsch theorem: for $q>n$, the immersions of an $n$-manifold $M$ into $\mathbb{R}^q$ satisfy the h-principle, and a formal immersion is an injective bundle map $TM\to\mathbb{R}^q$.

Nash-Kuiper theorem: a short embedding of a Riemannian manifold into a higher dimensional Euclidean space is $C^0$-approximated by $C^1$ isometric embeddings, an h-principle proved by [convex integration](c:convex-integration).
Non-example: symplectic embeddings of a ball $B^{2n}(R)$ into a thin cylinder $B^2(r)\times\mathbb{R}^{2n-2}$ with $r<R$ have formal solutions but no genuine ones, by Gromov's non-squeezing theorem.

reminder: A Hamiltonian diffeomorphism is the time-one map of the flow of a time-dependent [Hamiltonian vector field](c:hamiltonian-vector-field).
definition: Let $(M,\omega)$ be a [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold) and $H:[0,1]\times M\to\mathbb{R}$ a [smooth function](c:smooth-function). Let $X_t$ be the [Hamiltonian vector field](c:hamiltonian-vector-field) of $H_t=H(t,\cdot)$, given by $\iota_{X_t}\omega=dH_t$ up to a sign convention, and let $\varphi_t$ be its [flow](c:flow-of-a-vector-field), which exists up to time $1$. A Hamiltonian diffeomorphism is a map of the form $\varphi_1$, a [diffeomorphism](c:diffeomorph) of $M$.
examples: A rotation of the sphere $S^2$ about its axis is a time-one map of the Hamiltonian flow of the height function, for the area form.
On $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $\omega=dx\wedge dy$, the flow of $H=\tfrac12(x^2+y^2)$ rotates the plane, so each rotation is a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism.

Non-example: the translation of the torus $\mathbb{R}^2/\mathbb{Z}^2$ by $(1/2,0)$ preserves the area form but has no fixed point, while every Hamiltonian diffeomorphism of the torus has at least three fixed points.

steps: Let $\varphi_t$ be the flow of a Hamiltonian vector field $X_t$ on $(M,\omega)$, so that $\iota_{X_t}\omega=dH_t$.
Then $\frac{d}{dt}\varphi_t^*\omega=\varphi_t^*(d\,\iota_{X_t}\omega)=\varphi_t^*(ddH_t)=0$, so each $\varphi_t$ preserves $\omega$.
So the time-one map is a [symplectomorphism](c:symplectomorphism), a diffeomorphism that preserves $\omega$.
The Hamiltonian case adds that the map is the end of an isotopy generated by a Hamiltonian function.
links.why: It shows that Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms are the symplectomorphisms that come from a Hamiltonian isotopy.

reminder: The $s$-dimensional Hausdorff [measure](c:measure) of a set is the limit of the smallest sums of $s$-th powers of diameters of fine covers.
definition: Let $(X,d)$ be a [metric space](c:metric-space) and $s\ge 0$. For $A\subseteq X$ and $\delta>0$, let $\mathcal{H}^s_\delta(A)$ be the infimum of $\sum_i(\operatorname{diam}U_i)^s$ over all countable covers of $A$ by sets $U_i$ of [diameter](c:diameter) at most $\delta$. The Hausdorff measure is $\mathcal{H}^s(A)=\lim_{\delta\to 0}\mathcal{H}^s_\delta(A)=\sup_{\delta>0}\mathcal{H}^s_\delta(A)$, which is an [outer measure](c:outer-measure) whose restriction to the Borel sets is a [measure](c:measure).
examples: The measure $\mathcal{H}^0$ is the counting measure, and $\mathcal{H}^1$ of a rectifiable curve is its length.
On $\mathbb{R}^n$, the measure $\mathcal{H}^n$ is a constant multiple of [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure).
For the Cantor middle-thirds set, $\mathcal{H}^s$ is finite and positive at $s=\log 2/\log 3$, and it is $\infty$ below this exponent and $0$ above it.
Non-example: $\mathcal{H}^1$ on the plane is not area, because every set of positive area has $\mathcal{H}^1=\infty$.

steps: An [outer measure](c:outer-measure) is a monotone, countably subadditive set function with value $0$ on the empty set.
The function $A\mapsto\mathcal{H}^s(A)$ is monotone, because a cover of a larger set also covers a smaller set.
It is countably subadditive, because covers of the pieces combine into a cover of the union.
So $\mathcal{H}^s$ is an outer measure that is built from covers weighted by $(\operatorname{diam}U)^s$.
links.why: It shows that Hausdorff measure is an outer measure, so Carathéodory's construction gives a measure on Borel sets.

steps: Take $X=\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean metric and $s=n$, and compare with [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) $\mathcal{L}^n$.
By the isodiametric inequality, a set of diameter $d$ has volume at most $\omega_n(d/2)^n$, where $\omega_n$ is the volume of the unit ball.
So $\mathcal{H}^n=(2^n/\omega_n)\,\mathcal{L}^n$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, and Hausdorff measure extends this to metric spaces and to any exponent $s$.
links.why: It shows Hausdorff measure as Lebesgue measure extended to metric spaces and to non-integer dimensions.

reminder: In an [(∞,1)-topos](c:infinity-1-topos), the homotopy groups of an object are the $0$-truncations of its iterated loop objects.
definition: Let $\mathbf{H}$ be an [(∞,1)-topos](c:infinity-1-topos), $X$ an object of $\mathbf{H}$ and $x:*\to X$ a point. The object $\pi_0(X)$ is the $0$-truncation $\tau_0X$, and for $n\ge 1$ the homotopy group object is $\pi_n(X,x)=\tau_0\,\Omega^n_xX$, the $0$-truncation of the $n$-fold [loop space object](c:loop-space) of $X$ at $x$. For $n\ge 1$ this is a group object of $\mathbf{H}$, abelian for $n\ge 2$.
examples: In the (∞,1)-topos $\infty\mathrm{Grpd}$ of spaces, $\pi_0(X)$ is the set of components, and $\pi_n(X,x)$ are the usual [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group).
In the (∞,1)-topos of sheaves on a space, the stalks of $\pi_n(X,x)$ are the ordinary homotopy groups of the stalks of $X$.
Non-example: the homotopy groups of the space of global sections of $X$ are groups, not group objects of the topos, and they can differ from $\pi_n(X)$.

steps: Take $\mathbf{H}=\infty\mathrm{Grpd}$, the (∞,1)-topos of spaces up to homotopy.
The $0$-truncated objects of $\infty\mathrm{Grpd}$ are sets, so a group object there is an ordinary group.
The loop object $\Omega^n_xX$ is the usual $n$-fold loop space of $X$.
So $\tau_0\Omega^n_xX$ is the ordinary [homotopy group](c:homotopy-group) $\pi_n(X,x)$.
links.why: It shows that the topos version restricts to the familiar homotopy groups on spaces.

reminder: The Hopf invariant of a map $S^{2n-1}\to S^n$ is the [linking number](c:linking-number) of the preimages of two distinct regular values.
definition: Let $n\ge 2$ and let $f:S^{2n-1}\to S^n$ be a smooth map. The Hopf invariant $H(f)\in\mathbb{Z}$ is the [linking number](c:linking-number) of the preimages $f^{-1}(p)$ and $f^{-1}(q)$ of two distinct regular values $p$ and $q$. Equivalently, in the [mapping cone](c:mapping-cone) $C_f=S^n\cup_f e^{2n}$ with generators $a\in H^n$ and $b\in H^{2n}$, the [cup product](c:cup-product) satisfies $a\cup a=H(f)\,b$.
examples: The Hopf map $S^3\to S^2$ has Hopf invariant $1$: any two of its fibres are circles that link once.
Composing with a degree $k$ map on $S^n$ multiplies the Hopf invariant by $k^2$, and precomposing with a degree $k$ map on $S^{2n-1}$ multiplies it by $k$.
For odd $n$, as for maps $S^5\to S^3$, the Hopf invariant is always $0$, because $a\cup a=-a\cup a$.
Non-example: a map $S^4\to S^2$ has no Hopf invariant in this sense, because the source must be $S^{2n-1}$ when the target is $S^n$.

reminder: The Hopf link consists of two unknotted circles that link exactly once, so its [linking number](c:linking-number) is $\pm 1$.
definition: The Hopf link is the two-component [link](c:link) formed by an [unknot](c:unknot) and a circle that goes once around it, a meridian of the first component. Each component then bounds a disk that the other component meets once, so the [linking number](c:linking-number) is $\pm 1$ and depends on the orientations.
examples: Any two fibres of the [Hopf fibration](c:hopf-fibration) $S^3\to S^2$ form a Hopf link.
Two links of a chain, each hooked once through the other, model the Hopf link, and its standard diagram has two crossings.
Non-example: two disjoint round circles in the plane, one outside the other, form the unlink, whose linking number is $0$.

steps: Start with a [link](c:link) that has exactly two components.
Let the first component be an unknot $K_1$.
Let the second component be a meridian circle of $K_1$ that goes once around it.
Then each component bounds a disk that the other meets once, so the [linking number](c:linking-number) is $\pm 1$.
links.why: It shows what the Hopf link adds to a two-component link: one component is a meridian of the other.

reminder: Horizontal composition in a [2-category](c:2-category) joins two $2$-cells side by side along a common object.
definition: In a [2-category](c:2-category), let $\alpha:f\Rightarrow f'$ be a $2$-morphism between $1$-morphisms $f,f':A\to B$, and let $\beta:g\Rightarrow g'$ be one between $g,g':B\to C$. Their horizontal composite $\beta*\alpha:g\circ f\Rightarrow g'\circ f'$ is the $2$-morphism that composes along the object $B$. It satisfies the interchange law $(\beta'\cdot\beta)*(\alpha'\cdot\alpha)=(\beta'*\alpha')\cdot(\beta*\alpha)$ with [vertical composition](c:vertical-composition) $\cdot$.
examples: In the $2$-category $\mathrm{Cat}$ of categories, functors and natural transformations, the composite of $\alpha:F\Rightarrow F'$ and $\beta:G\Rightarrow G'$ has components $(\beta*\alpha)_X=\beta_{F'X}\circ G(\alpha_X)$, the [Godement product](c:godement-product).
In a monoidal category viewed as a $2$-category with one object, horizontal composition is the tensor product of morphisms.
Non-example: composing $\alpha:f\Rightarrow f'$ with $\alpha':f'\Rightarrow f''$ along the shared $1$-morphism $f'$ is vertical composition, not horizontal composition.

steps: Take the $2$-category $\mathrm{Cat}$: its objects are categories, its $1$-morphisms are functors, and its $2$-morphisms are [natural transformations](c:natural-transformation).
For $\alpha:F\Rightarrow F'$ and $\beta:G\Rightarrow G'$, horizontal composition gives $\beta*\alpha:GF\Rightarrow G'F'$.
Its component at $X$ is $\beta_{F'X}\circ G(\alpha_X)$.
This is exactly the [Godement product](c:godement-product) of natural transformations.
links.why: It shows that horizontal composition in any $2$-category is the Godement product made abstract.

steps: Take a $2$-morphism $\alpha:f\Rightarrow f'$ and a $1$-morphism $g:B\to C$.
Use the identity $2$-morphism $1_g:g\Rightarrow g$ as the second $2$-cell.
Then $1_g*\alpha:gf\Rightarrow gf'$ is the [whiskering](c:whiskering) of $\alpha$ by $g$.
links.why: It shows that whiskering is horizontal composition with an identity $2$-cell.

reminder: A hypersurface is a [submanifold](c:submanifold) of [codimension](c:codimension) one, such as the zero set of a single regular equation.
definition: A hypersurface in an $n$-dimensional [manifold](c:manifold) $M$ is a submanifold of dimension $n-1$, that is, of [codimension](c:codimension) $1$. Locally it is a level set $\{F=0\}$ of a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) $F$ whose differential is nonzero at each point of the set. In algebraic geometry, a hypersurface of affine $n$-space is the zero set of one nonconstant [polynomial](c:polynomial) in $n$ variables.
examples: The unit sphere $S^{n-1}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:|x|^2=1\}$ is a hypersurface of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The graph of a smooth function $g:\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\to\mathbb{R}$ is a hypersurface of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
In the plane the curve $y^2=x^3-x$ is an algebraic hypersurface, and in $\mathbb{R}^3$ a surface such as a paraboloid is one.
Non-example: a line in $\mathbb{R}^3$ has codimension $2$, so it is not a hypersurface.

steps: Start with an $n$-dimensional manifold $M$ and a [submanifold](c:submanifold) $S$ of $M$.
Add the condition that $\dim S=n-1$, so that $S$ has [codimension](c:codimension) one.
Then $S$ is a hypersurface.
links.why: It shows that a hypersurface is a submanifold with the largest possible dimension below that of $M$.

reminder: The identity function on a [set](c:set) sends every element to itself.
definition: For a [set](c:set) $S$, the identity function $\mathrm{id}_S:S\to S$ is the [function](c:function) with $\mathrm{id}_S(x)=x$ for every $x\in S$. It satisfies $f\circ\mathrm{id}_S=f$ and $\mathrm{id}_T\circ f=f$ for every function $f:S\to T$. Every point of $S$ is a [fixed point](c:fixed-point) of $\mathrm{id}_S$.
examples: On $\mathbb{R}$, the identity function has the line $y=x$ as its graph.
The identity function is the unit for composition: $\sin\circ\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}}=\sin$.
Non-example: the map $x\mapsto -x$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is not the identity, because it moves every point except $0$.

steps: Work in the category of sets, where the objects are sets and the morphisms are functions.
An [identity morphism](c:identity-morphism) of $S$ is a morphism $e:S\to S$ with $f\circ e=f$ and $e\circ g=g$ whenever the composites are defined.
The function $\mathrm{id}_S$ satisfies both laws, since $f(\mathrm{id}_S(x))=f(x)$.
So $\mathrm{id}_S$ is the identity morphism of $S$ in the category of sets.
links.why: It shows that the identity function is the identity morphism of the category of sets.

reminder: The Iitaka dimension of a [line bundle](c:line-bundle) $L$ is the largest dimension of the image of the [rational map](c:rational-map) given by sections of $L^{\otimes m}$.
definition: Let $L$ be a [line bundle](c:line-bundle) on a normal [projective variety](c:projective-variety) $X$. For $m\ge 1$ with $H^0(X,L^{\otimes m})\neq 0$, the sections give a [rational map](c:rational-map) $\varphi_m:X\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}(H^0(X,L^{\otimes m}))$. The Iitaka dimension $\kappa(X,L)$ is the largest dimension of the image of $\varphi_m$ over all such $m$, and it is $-\infty$ if no power of $L$ has a nonzero [global section](c:global-section).
examples: For an ample line bundle on a variety of dimension $n$, the Iitaka dimension is $n$.
The trivial bundle $\mathcal{O}_X$ has Iitaka dimension $0$, because every power has only constant sections, so the image is a point.
If $X=\mathbb{P}^1\times Y$ and $L$ is the pullback of $\mathcal{O}(1)$ from $\mathbb{P}^1$, then the Iitaka dimension is $1$.
Non-example: $\mathcal{O}(-1)$ on $\mathbb{P}^n$ gives no rational map, because no power has a nonzero section, so its Iitaka dimension is the symbol $-\infty$.

reminder: The index of a [linear map](c:linear-map) is the dimension of its [kernel](c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism) minus the dimension of its [cokernel](c:cokernel).
definition: Let $T:V\to W$ be a [linear map](c:linear-map) whose [kernel](c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism) and [cokernel](c:cokernel) are finite-dimensional. Its index is the integer $\operatorname{ind}T=\dim\ker T-\dim\operatorname{coker}T$, where $\dim$ is the [dimension](c:dimension-of-a-vector-space). For a map between finite-dimensional spaces, rank-nullity gives $\operatorname{ind}T=\dim V-\dim W$.
examples: Every linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional spaces has index $\dim V-\dim W$.
The right shift $(x_1,x_2,\dots)\mapsto(0,x_1,x_2,\dots)$ on $\ell^2$ has kernel $0$ and a one-dimensional cokernel, so its index is $-1$.
The left shift on $\ell^2$ has a one-dimensional kernel and zero cokernel, so its index is $1$.
Non-example: the zero operator on $\ell^2$ has an infinite-dimensional kernel and cokernel, so it has no index.

steps: Let $T:X\to Y$ be a [Fredholm operator](c:fredholm-operator) between Banach spaces.
Its kernel is finite-dimensional, and its range is closed with a finite-dimensional cokernel.
So $T$ is a linear map for which $\dim\ker T-\dim\operatorname{coker}T$ is defined.
This number is the [Fredholm index](c:fredholm-index) of $T$, so the Fredholm index is the index of operators with closed range.
links.why: It shows that the Fredholm index is the algebraic index applied to bounded operators.

steps: Let $D$ be a [Dirac operator](c:dirac-operator) on a closed manifold.
The operator $D$ is elliptic, so it is a Fredholm operator between Sobolev spaces.
Hence its kernel and cokernel are finite-dimensional, and $\dim\ker D-\dim\operatorname{coker}D$ is defined.
This number is the [index of the Dirac operator](c:index-of-a-dirac-operator).
links.why: It shows that the index of a Dirac operator is a special case of the index of a linear map.

reminder: An infinitary logic allows [formulas](c:formula) with conjunctions, disjunctions or quantifier blocks of infinite length.
definition: For infinite [cardinals](c:cardinal-number) $\kappa\ge\lambda$, the infinitary logic $L_{\kappa\lambda}$ builds [formulas](c:formula) like [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic), but it also allows conjunctions and disjunctions of fewer than $\kappa$ formulas and blocks of fewer than $\lambda$ quantifiers. The most used case is $L_{\omega_1\omega}$, with countable conjunctions and disjunctions and finite quantifier blocks. A structure satisfies an infinite conjunction when it satisfies every formula in it.
examples: In $L_{\omega_1\omega}$, the sentence $\forall x\bigvee_{n\ge 1}(x^n=1)$ says that a group is a torsion group.
In $L_{\omega_1\omega}$, the sentence $\forall x\bigvee_{n\in\mathbb{N}}x=S^n(0)$ says that every element is a standard numeral, which no first-order sentence expresses.
Non-example: in first-order logic, which allows only finite conjunctions, no set of sentences defines exactly the torsion groups.

steps: [First-order logic](c:first-order-logic) is the logic $L_{\omega\omega}$, in which every conjunction, disjunction and quantifier block is finite.
Raise the first bound from $\omega$ to $\omega_1$, and allow countable conjunctions and disjunctions.
The result is $L_{\omega_1\omega}$, and every first-order formula is a formula of it.
So infinitary logic keeps all first-order formulas and adds the infinite ones.
links.why: It shows that infinitary logic extends first-order logic by raising the allowed length of formulas.

reminder: An (∞,1)-presheaf on $C$ is an [(∞,1)-functor](c:infinity-1-functor) from the opposite of $C$ to the ∞-groupoids.
definition: Let $C$ be an [(∞,1)-category](c:infinity-1-category). An (∞,1)-presheaf on $C$ is an [(∞,1)-functor](c:infinity-1-functor) $F:C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\infty\mathrm{Grpd}$ from the [opposite](c:opposite-infinity-1-category) of $C$ to the (∞,1)-category of [∞-groupoids](c:infinity-groupoid). So $F$ assigns a space $F(c)$ to each object $c$ and a map $F(g):F(c')\to F(c)$ to each morphism $g:c\to c'$, coherently up to higher homotopy.
examples: For an object $c$ of $C$, the representable presheaf $\mathrm{Hom}_C(-,c)$ is an (∞,1)-presheaf, and $c\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}_C(-,c)$ is the Yoneda embedding.
If $C$ is a point, an (∞,1)-presheaf on $C$ is just an ∞-groupoid.
Non-example: an (∞,1)-functor $C\to\infty\mathrm{Grpd}$ with the wrong variance is a [copresheaf](c:copresheaf), not a presheaf on $C$.

steps: Let $F:C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{Set}$ be a [presheaf](c:presheaf) on an ordinary category $C$.
View $C$ as an (∞,1)-category through its nerve.
View each set $F(c)$ as a discrete ∞-groupoid, one with no higher homotopy.
Then $F$ is an (∞,1)-presheaf, and ordinary presheaves are the ones with discrete values.
links.why: It shows that (∞,1)-presheaves extend ordinary presheaves by allowing spaces instead of sets.

steps: Take an [(∞,1)-functor](c:infinity-1-functor) $F:D\to E$.
Choose $D=C^{\mathrm{op}}$ and $E=\infty\mathrm{Grpd}$.
Then $F$ is an (∞,1)-presheaf on $C$.
links.why: It shows that a presheaf is a functor with a fixed source and a fixed target.

reminder: An algebra over an [(∞,1)-operad](c:infinity-1-operad) $O$ is a morphism of (∞,1)-operads from $O$ to a symmetric monoidal (∞,1)-category.
definition: Let $O$ be an [(∞,1)-operad](c:infinity-1-operad) and $\mathcal{C}$ a [symmetric monoidal (∞,1)-category](c:symmetric-monoidal-infinity-1-category). An $O$-algebra in $\mathcal{C}$ is a morphism of (∞,1)-operads $A:O\to\mathcal{C}$. It gives an object of $\mathcal{C}$ for each color of $O$ and a morphism $A(c_1)\otimes\cdots\otimes A(c_n)\to A(c)$ for each operation, and the composition laws of $O$ hold up to coherent higher homotopy.
examples: Algebras over the associative operad $E_1$ in spectra are $A_\infty$-ring spectra, and algebras over the commutative operad $E_\infty$ are $E_\infty$-ring spectra.
Every $n$-fold loop space $\Omega^nX$ is an algebra over the [little cubes operad](c:little-cubes-operad) $E_n$ in spaces.
Non-example: a ring spectrum whose multiplication is commutative only up to homotopy, with no higher coherence data, is not an $E_\infty$-algebra.

steps: Let $O$ be an ordinary [operad](c:operad) of sets and $\mathcal{C}$ an ordinary symmetric monoidal category, such as vector spaces.
View $O$ as an (∞,1)-operad and $\mathcal{C}$ as a symmetric monoidal (∞,1)-category, both through their nerves.
An algebra $O\to\mathcal{C}$ in the ordinary sense is then a morphism of (∞,1)-operads.
So an ordinary algebra over an operad is an ∞-algebra whose higher coherences are all strict.
links.why: It shows that ∞-algebras extend ordinary operad algebras by letting the laws hold up to coherent homotopy.

steps: Take the (∞,1)-operad $E_1$, the little $1$-cubes operad.
An $E_1$-algebra in $\mathcal{C}$ is an object with a multiplication that is associative up to coherent homotopy.
That is an [A-infinity algebra](c:a-infinity-algebra), so these algebras are the case $O=E_1$.
links.why: It shows that A-infinity algebras are the ∞-algebras over the associative operad.

reminder: An ∞-topos is a left exact localization of an (∞,1)-category of [(∞,1)-presheaves](c:infinity-1-presheaf).
definition: An ∞-topos is an [(∞,1)-category](c:infinity-1-category) $\mathbf{H}$ with a left exact, accessible localization functor $\mathrm{PSh}(C)\to\mathbf{H}$ from the category of [(∞,1)-presheaves](c:infinity-1-presheaf) on a small (∞,1)-category $C$. Equivalently, by the Giraud axioms, $\mathbf{H}$ is presentable, colimits are universal, coproducts are disjoint, and groupoid objects are effective.
examples: The (∞,1)-category $\infty\mathrm{Grpd}$ of ∞-groupoids is an ∞-topos: it is the presheaf category on a point.
For a topological space or a site $S$, the (∞,1)-category of [(∞,1)-sheaves](c:infinity-1-sheaf) on $S$ is an ∞-topos.
Non-example: the (∞,1)-category of spectra is not an ∞-topos, because it is pointed, so its initial object is terminal, while coproducts in an ∞-topos are disjoint.

steps: Take a site $C$ and form the ∞-topos of ∞-sheaves on $C$.
Restrict to its $0$-truncated objects, the ones with trivial higher homotopy.
These objects form the ordinary [Grothendieck topos](c:grothendieck-topos) of sheaves of sets on $C$.
So every Grothendieck topos is the $0$-truncated part of an ∞-topos, which adds higher homotopy.
links.why: It shows how an ∞-topos extends an ordinary topos by objects with higher homotopy.

reminder: A [form](c:differential-form) is an integral invariant of a flow when its integrals over chains do not change as the flow moves the chains.
definition: Let $\varphi_t$ be the [flow](c:flow-of-a-vector-field) of a [vector field](c:vector-field) on a manifold $M$, and let $\alpha$ be a $k$-[differential form](c:differential-form). The form $\alpha$ is an absolute integral invariant when $\int_{\varphi_t(\sigma)}\alpha=\int_\sigma\alpha$ for every $k$-chain $\sigma$ and every $t$, which holds exactly when $\varphi_t^*\alpha=\alpha$. It is a relative integral invariant when this holds only for closed chains $\sigma$, which means that $\varphi_t^*\alpha-\alpha$ is exact.
examples: The symplectic form $\omega$ is an absolute integral invariant of every Hamiltonian flow, because these flows preserve $\omega$.
The one-form $p\,dq$ is a relative integral invariant of a time-independent Hamiltonian flow, because $\varphi_t^*(p\,dq)-p\,dq$ is exact.

Non-example: the area form $dx\wedge dy$ is not an absolute integral invariant of the dilation flow $\varphi_t(x,y)=(e^tx,e^ty)$, because $\varphi_t^*(dx\wedge dy)=e^{2t}\,dx\wedge dy$ and the area of a disk grows.

reminder: An invariant eigendistribution is a [distribution](c:distribution) on a Lie group that conjugation fixes and the center of the enveloping algebra scales.
definition: Let $G$ be a real [reductive group](c:reductive-group) with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$, and let $\mathfrak{Z}$ be the center of the [universal enveloping algebra](c:universal-enveloping-algebra) of $\mathfrak{g}$, which acts on [distributions](c:distribution) on $G$ by invariant differential operators. A distribution $T$ on $G$ is an invariant eigendistribution when it is invariant under [conjugation](c:conjugation) by $G$ and there is a character $\chi:\mathfrak{Z}\to\mathbb{C}$ with $zT=\chi(z)T$ for every $z\in\mathfrak{Z}$.
examples: The character $\Theta_\pi$ of an irreducible admissible representation $\pi$ of $G$ is an invariant eigendistribution, by a theorem of Harish-Chandra.
For $G=\mathbb{R}$, every exponential $e^{\lambda x}$ is an invariant eigendistribution, because conjugation is trivial and $\frac{d}{dx}e^{\lambda x}=\lambda e^{\lambda x}$.

Non-example: the Dirac delta $\delta_e$ at the identity is invariant under conjugation, but it is not an eigendistribution, because a second-order element of $\mathfrak{Z}$ sends it to a distribution of order $2$.

reminder: A subspace is invariant under a linear map when the map sends every vector of the subspace back into the subspace.
definition: Let $T:V\to V$ be a [linear map](c:linear-map) of a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$. A [linear subspace](c:linear-subspace) $W\subseteq V$ is $T$-invariant when $T(W)\subseteq W$, that is, $Tw\in W$ for every $w\in W$. Then $T$ restricts to a linear map $W\to W$ and induces a linear map on the quotient $V/W$.
examples: The subspaces $\{0\}$ and $V$ are invariant under every $T$, and so are $\ker T$ and $\operatorname{im}T$.
The span of an [eigenvector](c:eigenvector) is a one-dimensional invariant subspace, and every [eigenspace](c:eigenspace) is invariant.
Non-example: for the rotation of $\mathbb{R}^2$ by $90^\circ$, the $x$-axis is not invariant, because the rotation sends it to the $y$-axis.

steps: Let $\lambda$ be an [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue) of $T$, and let $E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda)$ be its [eigenspace](c:eigenspace).
For $v\in E_\lambda$ we have $Tv=\lambda v$, which lies in $E_\lambda$.
So $E_\lambda$ is a $T$-invariant subspace, and $T$ acts on it as multiplication by $\lambda$.
A general invariant subspace drops the requirement that $T$ acts as a scalar.
links.why: It shows that eigenspaces are the invariant subspaces on which the map acts by one scalar.

reminder: A system of partial differential equations is involutive when no new conditions appear after prolongation and its symbol is involutive.
definition: Let $\mathcal{R}$ be a system of [partial differential equations](c:partial-differential-equation), viewed as a subbundle of a [jet bundle](c:jet-bundle). Its [prolongation](c:jet-prolongation) $\mathcal{R}^{(k)}$ adds the derivatives of the equations up to order $k$ more. The system is involutive when it is formally integrable, so that each $\mathcal{R}^{(k)}$ projects onto $\mathcal{R}^{(k-1)}$, and its symbol is involutive, that is, it passes Cartan's test.
examples: The Cauchy-Riemann equations $u_x=v_y$ and $u_y=-v_x$ form an involutive system.
The single equation $u_x=0$ for $u(x,y)$ is involutive, and its solutions are the functions $u(y)$.
Non-example: the system $u_x=y$, $u_y=0$ is not involutive, because crossing the derivatives gives $1=0$, a new condition of lower order.

reminder: An open immersion is an open embedding of spaces that also identifies the [structure sheaf](c:structure-sheaf) of the source with a restriction of the target's sheaf.
definition: A morphism $f:X\to Y$ of [ringed spaces](c:ringed-space), such as [schemes](c:scheme), is an open immersion when the map of underlying spaces is an [open embedding](c:is-open-embedding) onto an open set $U\subseteq Y$, and for every open $V\subseteq U$ the sheaf map $\mathcal{O}_Y(V)\to\mathcal{O}_X(f^{-1}V)$ is an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism). In other words, $f$ is an isomorphism from $X$ onto the open subspace $U$ with the restricted structure sheaf.
examples: For a ring $A$ and $f\in A$, the map $\operatorname{Spec}A_f\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ is an open immersion onto the basic open set $D(f)$.
The inclusion of an open subset $U\subseteq X$ of a scheme, with the restricted structure sheaf, is an open immersion.
Non-example: the closed immersion $\operatorname{Spec}k[x]/(x)\to\operatorname{Spec}k[x]$ is an embedding of spaces, but its image $\{0\}$ is not open.

steps: Forget the structure sheaves of $X$ and $Y$.
An open immersion then gives an [open embedding](c:is-open-embedding) of the underlying topological spaces.
The ringed case adds the condition that $\mathcal{O}_Y|_U\to f_*\mathcal{O}_X$ is an isomorphism.
links.why: It shows that an open immersion is an open embedding that also respects the sheaves of functions.

steps: Recall that an [immersion of schemes](c:is-immersion) is a closed immersion into an open subscheme.
Let $f$ be an open immersion onto the open subscheme $U$.
Then $f:X\to U$ is an isomorphism, which is a closed immersion.
So $f$ is an immersion, and the open case adds that the closed part is an isomorphism.
links.why: It shows that open immersions are the immersions with no closed part.

reminder: A knot is an embedded [circle](c:circle) in three-dimensional space, taken up to isotopy.
definition: A knot is a [smooth embedding](c:embedding-of-differentiable-manifolds) $K:S^1\to\mathbb{R}^3$ of the [circle](c:circle), or into the [sphere](c:sphere) $S^3$, identified with its image. Two knots are equivalent when an ambient [smooth isotopy](c:smooth-isotopy) carries one to the other, and the unknot is the class of a round circle.
examples: The unknot is a round circle, and the [trefoil knot](c:trefoil-knot) and the [figure-eight knot](c:figure-eight-knot) are the simplest nontrivial knots.
The $(p,q)$ torus knot lies on a standard torus and winds $p$ times one way and $q$ times the other way; the trefoil is the $(2,3)$ torus knot.
Non-example: a closed curve with a double point, such as a figure eight drawn with a crossing point, is not an embedding, so it is not a knot.

steps: A [link](c:link) is an embedding of a disjoint union of circles into $\mathbb{R}^3$ or $S^3$.
Take a link with exactly one component.
Its single component is an embedded circle in three-dimensional space.
So a knot is a link with one component.
links.why: It shows that knot theory is the one-component case of link theory.

steps: Take the circle $S^1$ as the source manifold and $\mathbb{R}^3$ as the target.
A smooth embedding $S^1\to\mathbb{R}^3$ is a knot.
The knot case adds the equivalence of embeddings up to ambient isotopy.
links.why: It shows that a knot is a smooth embedding of a circle, studied up to isotopy.

reminder: The Kontsevich integral is a universal [Vassiliev invariant](c:vassiliev-invariant) of knots, given by an iterated integral with values in chord diagrams.
definition: The Kontsevich integral $Z(K)$ of a [knot](c:knot) $K$ is an iterated integral over $K$ with values in the completed algebra of [chord diagrams](c:chord-diagram) modulo the 4T relation. Its degree $m$ part sums, over all choices of $m$ pairs of points of $K$ at equal heights $t_1<\dots<t_m$, the chord diagram of the pairs with the form $\frac{1}{(2\pi i)^m}\prod_j d\log(z_j-z_j')$ and a sign. It is built from the [holonomy](c:holonomy) of the [Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov equation](c:knizhnik-zamolodchikov-equation) along the knot, after normalization, and it is a [universal Vassiliev invariant](c:universal-vassiliev-invariant).
examples: Composing $Z$ with the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ [weight system](c:lie-algebra-weight-system) gives the Jones polynomial as a power series in $h=\log q$.
The degree $2$ part of $Z$ carries the second coefficient of the Conway polynomial, which is a Vassiliev invariant of degree $2$.
Non-example: the number of crossings of a knot diagram is not a knot invariant, so it is not a coefficient of $Z$.

steps: A [universal Vassiliev invariant](c:universal-vassiliev-invariant) is a knot invariant, valued in chord diagrams, that gives every Vassiliev invariant after a weight system is applied.
The Kontsevich integral is a knot invariant valued in the completed algebra of chord diagrams.
Applying a weight system to it gives a Vassiliev invariant, and every Vassiliev invariant arises this way.
So it is a universal Vassiliev invariant, the one given by an explicit iterated integral.
links.why: It shows that the Kontsevich integral is one explicit universal Vassiliev invariant.

reminder: A Laurent polynomial is a finite sum of terms $a_it^i$ in which the exponents may be negative integers.
definition: A Laurent polynomial over a [ring](c:ring) $R$ in the variable $t$ is a finite sum $\sum_{i=-m}^{n}a_it^i$ with $a_i\in R$ and integers $m,n\ge 0$. The Laurent polynomials form the ring $R[t,t^{-1}]$, in which $t$ is invertible; with $k$ variables one writes $R[t_1^{\pm 1},\dots,t_k^{\pm 1}]$.
examples: The sum $t^{-2}+3+5t$ is a Laurent polynomial over $\mathbb{Z}$.
Every [polynomial](c:polynomial) is a Laurent polynomial, and $\mathbb{R}[t,t^{-1}]$ is the group ring of $\mathbb{Z}$ over $\mathbb{R}$.
Non-example: $1/(1+t)$ is not a Laurent polynomial, and neither is $\sum_{n\ge 0}t^{-n}$, because it has infinitely many terms.

steps: Let $p=\sum_{i=0}^{n}a_it^i$ be a [polynomial](c:polynomial) over $R$.
Its exponents are nonnegative integers, so $p$ is also a finite sum of terms $a_it^i$ with integer exponents.
So $p$ is a Laurent polynomial with no negative exponents.
The Laurent case allows negative exponents, which makes $t$ invertible.
links.why: It shows that a Laurent polynomial is a polynomial in $t$ and $t^{-1}$ together.

steps: Take the group $\mathbb{Z}^k$ and a ring $R$, and form the [group ring](c:group-ring) $R[\mathbb{Z}^k]$.
Write the basis element $(i_1,\dots,i_k)$ as the monomial $t_1^{i_1}\cdots t_k^{i_k}$.
Multiplication of basis elements adds the exponents, so the product of monomials is the usual one.
So the group ring $R[\mathbb{Z}^k]$ is the ring of Laurent polynomials in $k$ variables.
links.why: It shows that Laurent polynomial rings are the group rings of the free abelian groups.

reminder: A leaf of a [foliation](c:foliation) is a maximal connected submanifold that is tangent to the foliation.
definition: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a [foliation](c:foliation) of a [manifold](c:manifold) $M$, so that $M$ is covered by charts in which $\mathcal{F}$ is cut into parallel plaques. Two points lie in the same leaf when a chain of plaques joins them, and each leaf is a maximal connected, injectively immersed [submanifold](c:submanifold) tangent to $\mathcal{F}$. For a trivial [covering space](c:covering-space) $E|_U\cong U\times F$, the sheets $U\times\{f\}$, indexed by the elements $f$ of $F$, are the leaves over $U$.
examples: For the foliation of $\mathbb{R}^2$ by horizontal lines, the leaves are the lines $y=c$.
For the foliation of the torus $\mathbb{R}^2/\mathbb{Z}^2$ by lines of irrational slope, each leaf is a dense copy of $\mathbb{R}$, so it is immersed but not embedded.
Non-example: an open segment of a horizontal line is not a leaf of the foliation of the plane by horizontal lines, because it is not maximal.

reminder: The Leray [spectral sequence](c:spectral-sequence) of $f:X\to Y$ and a sheaf $F$ has $E_2^{p,q}=H^p(Y,R^qf_*F)$ and converges to $H^{p+q}(X,F)$.
definition: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a [continuous function](c:continuous-function) of topological spaces and $F$ a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$. The Leray spectral sequence is the [Grothendieck spectral sequence](c:grothendieck-spectral-sequence) of the composite $\Gamma(X,-)=\Gamma(Y,-)\circ f_*$. It has $E_2^{p,q}=H^p(Y,R^qf_*F)$, where $R^qf_*F$ is the $q$-th higher [direct image](c:direct-image) of $F$, and it converges to the [sheaf cohomology](c:abelian-sheaf-cohomology) $H^{p+q}(X,F)$.
examples: If $f$ is a closed embedding, then $R^qf_*F=0$ for $q>0$, and the sequence collapses to $H^p(Y,f_*F)=H^p(X,F)$.

For a fibre bundle $f:X\to Y$ with fibre $\Phi$ and $F=\underline{\mathbb{Z}}$, the sheaf $R^qf_*F$ is the local system of $H^q(\Phi,\mathbb{Z})$, which gives the [Serre spectral sequence](c:serre-spectral-sequence).
Non-example: the Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequence is not a Leray spectral sequence, because it comes from a skeletal filtration, with no map $f$ and no higher direct images.

steps: The Grothendieck spectral sequence starts from left exact functors $G$ and $H$ in which $G$ sends injective objects to $H$-acyclic objects.
Take $G=f_*$ on sheaves of abelian groups and $H=\Gamma(Y,-)$, so that $H\circ G=\Gamma(X,-)$.
The functor $f_*$ sends injectives to injectives, because its left adjoint $f^{-1}$ is exact.
So the Grothendieck sequence exists and has $E_2^{p,q}=H^p(Y,R^qf_*F)$, which is the Leray spectral sequence.
links.why: It shows that the Leray spectral sequence is the Grothendieck spectral sequence for pushforward followed by global sections.

steps: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a fibre bundle with fibre $\Phi$ over a nice base.
The sheaf $R^qf_*\underline{\mathbb{Z}}$ is the locally constant sheaf with stalk $H^q(\Phi,\mathbb{Z})$.
So $E_2^{p,q}=H^p(Y,\mathcal{H}^q(\Phi))$, with coefficients in this local system.
This is the [Serre spectral sequence](c:serre-spectral-sequence), so the Leray sequence covers maps that are not fibre bundles too.
links.why: It shows that the Serre spectral sequence is the Leray spectral sequence of a fibre bundle.

reminder: A Lie algebra action on a manifold is a Lie algebra homomorphism from the Lie algebra to the vector fields on the manifold.
definition: An action of a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{g}$ on a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ is a homomorphism of Lie algebras $\rho:\mathfrak{g}\to\mathfrak{X}(M)$ into the Lie algebra of [vector fields](c:vector-field) on $M$ with the bracket of vector fields. So $\rho$ is linear and satisfies $\rho([x,y])=[\rho(x),\rho(y)]$ for all $x,y\in\mathfrak{g}$. The action is complete when every vector field $\rho(x)$ is complete.
examples: Every vector field $X$ gives an action of the abelian Lie algebra $\mathbb{R}$ by $t\mapsto tX$.
The three rotation fields $y\partial_z-z\partial_y$, $z\partial_x-x\partial_z$ and $x\partial_y-y\partial_x$ span a copy of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ that acts on $\mathbb{R}^3$.
Every [Lie group action](c:lie-group-action) differentiates to a Lie algebra action, up to a sign convention for the bracket.

Non-example: let a $2$-dimensional Lie algebra have $[e,f]=f$; the assignment $e\mapsto\partial_x$, $f\mapsto\partial_y$ is not an action, because $[\partial_x,\partial_y]=0$ but $\rho(f)=\partial_y\neq 0$.

steps: Let $\sigma:\mathfrak{g}\to\mathfrak{gl}(V)$ be a [Lie algebra representation](c:lie-algebra-representation) on a finite-dimensional vector space $V$.
Send $x$ to minus the linear vector field $v\mapsto\sigma(x)v$ on $V$, where the sign makes the brackets match.
This is a Lie algebra action of $\mathfrak{g}$ on the manifold $V$ by linear vector fields.
So an action on a manifold generalizes a representation, which is the linear case.
links.why: It shows that representations are the Lie algebra actions on vector spaces by linear vector fields.

steps: Let $X$ be a [vector field](c:vector-field) on $M$.
Define $\rho:\mathbb{R}\to\mathfrak{X}(M)$ by $\rho(t)=tX$.
The Lie algebra $\mathbb{R}$ has zero bracket, and $[tX,sX]=0$, so $\rho$ is a homomorphism.
So a single vector field is an action of the Lie algebra $\mathbb{R}$.
links.why: It shows that a single vector field is the case of an action by a one-dimensional Lie algebra.

reminder: A Lie group action is a smooth map $G\times M\to M$ by which a [Lie group](c:lie-group) acts on a manifold.
definition: An action of a [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$ on a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ is a [smooth map](c:smooth-map) $G\times M\to M$, $(g,x)\mapsto g\cdot x$, with $e\cdot x=x$ and $(gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$ for all $g,h\in G$ and $x\in M$. So it is a [group action](c:group-action) in which the action map is smooth in both variables, and each map $x\mapsto g\cdot x$ is a diffeomorphism.
examples: The rotation group $SO(n)$ acts on the sphere $S^{n-1}$ by $A\cdot x=Ax$.
Every Lie group acts on itself by left multiplication and by conjugation.
Non-example: the rule $t\cdot x=x+t^2$ for $t\in\mathbb{R}$ is smooth but not an action, because $(s+t)\cdot x\neq s\cdot(t\cdot x)$.

steps: A [group action](c:group-action) of $G$ on a set $X$ is a map $G\times X\to X$ with $e\cdot x=x$ and $(gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$.
Let $G$ be a Lie group and let $X$ be a smooth manifold.
Require that the action map $G\times X\to X$ is smooth.
Then each $g$ acts by a diffeomorphism, with inverse given by $g^{-1}$.
links.why: It shows what a Lie group action adds to a group action: smoothness, so each element acts by a diffeomorphism.

reminder: The little $k$-cubes operad has as $n$-ary operations the ways to place $n$ disjoint little cubes inside the unit cube.
definition: The little $k$-cubes operad $\mathcal{C}_k$ is the topological [operad](c:operad) whose space $\mathcal{C}_k(n)$ of $n$-ary operations is the space of $n$-tuples of rectilinear [embeddings](c:embedding-of-topological-spaces) $(0,1)^k\to(0,1)^k$ with disjoint images. Composition inserts a configuration of little cubes into one cube of another configuration by composing the embeddings. It is also called the $E_k$ operad, and it is a [topological operad](c:topological-operad) that acts on $k$-fold loop spaces.
examples: The space $\mathcal{C}_1(2)$ has two contractible components, one for each order of the two little intervals, and $\mathcal{C}_1$ is an [A-infinity operad](c:a-infinity-operad).
The space $\mathcal{C}_k(2)$ is homotopy equivalent to the sphere $S^{k-1}$.
Every $k$-fold loop space $\Omega^kX$ is an algebra over $\mathcal{C}_k$.
Non-example: two cubes with overlapping interiors do not give a point of $\mathcal{C}_k(2)$, because the images must be disjoint.

reminder: A local [observable](c:observable) of a field theory integrates a function of the field and its derivatives against a test function.
definition: Let $E\to X$ be the [field bundle](c:field-bundle) over spacetime $X$, and let the field configurations be the smooth sections $\Phi$ of $E$. A local [observable](c:observable) is a functional $\Phi\mapsto\int_X\chi(x)\,L(j^k_x\Phi)\,\mathrm{dvol}$, where $\chi$ is a compactly supported [bump function](c:bump-function), $j^k_x\Phi$ is the $k$-jet of the field at $x$ in the [jet bundle](c:jet-bundle), and $L$ is a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) on the jet bundle.
examples: For a scalar field $\phi$, the smeared field $\phi(\chi)=\int\chi\,\phi\,\mathrm{dvol}$ is a local observable.
An interaction term $\int\chi\,\phi^4\,\mathrm{dvol}$ is a local observable, and so is the smeared kinetic term $\int\chi\,(\partial\phi)^2\,\mathrm{dvol}$.
Non-example: the functional $\Phi\mapsto\phi(x)\phi(y)$ with $x\neq y$ depends on the field at two points, so it is not a local observable.

steps: An [observable](c:observable) is a function on the space of field configurations.
Take an observable of the form $\Phi\mapsto\int_X\chi\,L(j^k\Phi)\,\mathrm{dvol}$.
Here $\chi$ has compact support, and $L$ depends on the field and finitely many derivatives at one point.
Then the observable is local, because it uses the field only in a small region, one point at a time.
links.why: It shows what locality adds to an observable: it integrates a function of the jet at each point.

reminder: The mapping cone of $f:X\to Y$ is $Y$ with the cone on $X$ glued in along $f$, a model of the homotopy cofiber.
definition: For a map $f:X\to Y$ of [topological spaces](c:topological-space), the mapping cone is the [quotient space](c:quotient-space) $C_f=Y\cup_f CX$, where $CX=X\times[0,1]/X\times\{1\}$ and the point $(x,0)$ is identified with $f(x)$. It is a model of the homotopy [cofiber](c:cofiber) of $f$, and it sits in a cofiber sequence $X\to Y\to C_f\to\Sigma X$. For a map $f:X_\bullet\to Y_\bullet$ of [chain complexes](c:chain-complex), the cone has $C_n=X_{n-1}\oplus Y_n$ and $d(x,y)=(-dx,\,f(x)+dy)$.
examples: For $f:S^{n-1}\to Y$, the mapping cone $C_f$ is $Y$ with an $n$-cell attached along $f$.
If $f:X\to *$ is the map to a point, then $C_f$ is the unreduced [suspension](c:suspension) of $X$.
Non-example: the mapping cylinder $(X\times[0,1])\cup_f Y$ is homotopy equivalent to $Y$ and is not the mapping cone, because its end $X\times\{1\}$ is not collapsed.

steps: Let $X$ be a space and let $f:X\to *$ be the map to a point.
The mapping cone is $C_f=*\cup_f CX$, which is the cone $CX$ with its base $X\times\{0\}$ collapsed to a point.
Collapsing the base of a cone gives the [suspension](c:suspension) of $X$.
So the suspension is the mapping cone of $X\to *$, and a general mapping cone replaces the point by any space $Y$.
links.why: It shows that the suspension is the mapping cone of the map to a point.

reminder: A Mathieu group is one of the five sporadic simple groups $M_{11},M_{12},M_{22},M_{23},M_{24}$ of highly transitive permutations.
definition: The Mathieu group $M_{24}$ is the [automorphism group](c:automorphism-group) of the [Steiner system](c:steiner-system) $S(5,8,24)$ on $24$ points, which is also the [permutation group](c:permutation-group) of the coordinates that preserves the extended [binary Golay code](c:binary-golay-code). The group $M_{23}$ is the stabilizer of a point, and $M_{22}$ is the stabilizer of two points. The groups $M_{12}$ and $M_{11}$ arise in the same way from the Steiner system $S(5,6,12)$, with $M_{11}$ the stabilizer of a point of $M_{12}$.
examples: The group $M_{24}$ acts $5$-transitively on $24$ points, and $M_{12}$ acts $5$-transitively on $12$ points.
Non-example: the alternating group $A_{24}$ is also $5$-transitive on $24$ points, but it does not preserve the Steiner system, so it is not $M_{24}$.

steps: A [finite simple group](c:finite-simple-group) is a finite group with no proper nontrivial normal subgroup.
The Mathieu groups are finite simple groups.
They are not cyclic, alternating or of Lie type, which are the infinite families in the classification.
So each Mathieu group is a sporadic simple group, and it is one of the five earliest ones.
links.why: It shows that the Mathieu groups are the first sporadic groups, outside the infinite families.

reminder: A meager set is a countable union of [nowhere dense sets](c:nowhere-dense-set).
definition: A subset $A$ of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is meager, or of first category, when $A=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}N_n$ is a [countable](c:countable-set) union of [nowhere dense sets](c:nowhere-dense-set) $N_n$. A set is nowhere dense when the closure of the set has empty interior. A set that is not meager is nonmeager, or of second category.
examples: In $\mathbb{R}$, the set $\mathbb{Q}$ is meager, because it is a countable union of single points, and each point is nowhere dense.
The Cantor set is nowhere dense in $\mathbb{R}$, so it is meager.
Non-example: by the Baire category theorem, $\mathbb{R}$ is not meager in itself, and neither is any nonempty open interval.

steps: Let $N$ be a [nowhere dense set](c:nowhere-dense-set) in a space $X$.
Write $N=\bigcup_nN_n$ with $N_n=N$ for every $n$.
This is a countable union of nowhere dense sets, so $N$ is meager.
A general meager set also allows a countable union of different nowhere dense sets.
links.why: It shows that every nowhere dense set is meager, and that meager sets are the countable unions of such sets.

reminder: The mean value of an integrable function on a set is its [integral](c:integral) divided by the size of the set.
definition: Let $f$ be an integrable function on a set $S$ of finite [measure](c:measure) $\mu(S)>0$. The mean value of $f$ on $S$ is $\frac{1}{\mu(S)}\int_Sf\,d\mu$. On an interval $[a,b]$ it is $\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^bf(x)\,dx$, and on a circle of radius $r$ it is $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f(re^{i\theta})\,d\theta$.
examples: The mean value of $x^2$ on $[0,1]$ is $\int_0^1x^2\,dx=1/3$.
The mean value of $\sin x$ over $[0,2\pi]$ is $0$.
Hardy's theorem concerns the mean values $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f(re^{i\theta})|^p\,d\theta$ of a holomorphic function $f$ on circles of radius $r$.
Non-example: the value of $x^2$ at the midpoint of $[0,1]$ is $1/4$, which is not its mean value $1/3$.

steps: Let $(\Omega,P)$ be a probability space, so that $P(\Omega)=1$.
Let $X$ be an integrable random variable on $\Omega$.
The mean value of $X$ on $\Omega$ is $\frac{1}{P(\Omega)}\int X\,dP=\int X\,dP$.
This is the [expected value](c:expected-value) $E[X]$, so the expected value is the mean value for a probability measure.
links.why: It shows that the expected value is the mean value when the total measure is one.

reminder: A medial quasigroup is a [quasigroup](c:quasigroup) in which $(xy)(uv)=(xu)(yv)$ holds for all elements.
definition: A [quasigroup](c:quasigroup) $(Q,\cdot)$ is medial when $(x\cdot y)\cdot(u\cdot v)=(x\cdot u)\cdot(y\cdot v)$ for all $x,y,u,v\in Q$. By the Bruck-Toyoda theorem, $Q$ is medial exactly when, up to isomorphism, $x\cdot y=\varphi(x)+\psi(y)+c$ for an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) $(A,+)$, commuting [automorphisms](c:automorphism) $\varphi$ and $\psi$ of $A$, and an element $c\in A$.
examples: Every abelian group is a medial quasigroup, because $(x+y)+(u+v)=(x+u)+(y+v)$.
On $\mathbb{Z}_5$, the operation $x\cdot y=2x+3y$ is a medial quasigroup, with $\varphi=2$ and $\psi=3$.
Non-example: the symmetric group $S_3$ is a quasigroup under composition but it is not medial, because a medial group is abelian.

steps: Let $(Q,\cdot)$ be a [quasigroup](c:quasigroup): a set where each equation $a\cdot x=b$ and $y\cdot a=b$ has a unique solution.
Add the medial law $(x\cdot y)\cdot(u\cdot v)=(x\cdot u)\cdot(y\cdot v)$ for all elements.
A quasigroup that satisfies this law is a medial quasigroup.
links.why: It shows what mediality adds to a quasigroup: the entropic law for products of products.

steps: Let $(A,+)$ be an [abelian group](c:abelian-group); it is a quasigroup, because $a+x=b$ has the unique solution $x=b-a$.
Commutativity and associativity give $(x+y)+(u+v)=(x+u)+(y+v)$.
So $(A,+)$ is a medial quasigroup, and a medial quasigroup also allows operations such as $x-y$ or $\varphi(x)+\psi(y)$.
links.why: It shows that medial quasigroups are abelian groups with the operation twisted by automorphisms.

reminder: A mere proposition is a [type](c:type) in which any two elements are equal.
definition: A [type](c:type) $P$ is a mere proposition, or h-proposition, when any two elements of $P$ are equal: there is a term of the type $\prod_{x,y:P}(x=y)$, where $=$ is the [identity type](c:identity-type). Equivalently, $P$ is [contractible](c:contractible-type) as soon as it has an element, so $P$ carries no data beyond whether it is inhabited.
examples: The empty type and the unit type are mere propositions.
For natural numbers $m$ and $n$, the type $m\le n$ is a mere proposition.
For every type $A$, the type $\mathrm{isContr}(A)$ is a mere proposition.
Non-example: the type $\mathrm{Bool}$ is not a mere proposition, because the type $\mathrm{true}=\mathrm{false}$ has no element.

steps: Let $A$ be a [contractible type](c:contractible-type): it has a center $c:A$ with $x=c$ for every $x:A$.
For $x,y:A$, combine $x=c$ with the inverse of $y=c$ to get an identification $x=y$.
So $A$ is a mere proposition.
A mere proposition may also be empty, which a contractible type never is.
links.why: It shows that mere propositions are the types that are contractible whenever they are inhabited.

reminder: A mod $p$ representation is a [representation](c:group-representation) of a group on a vector space over a field of characteristic $p$.
definition: A mod $p$ representation of a group $G$ is a [group representation](c:group-representation) $\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ on a vector space $V$ over a field of [characteristic](c:characteristic) $p$, usually the [finite field](c:finite-field) $\mathbb{F}_p$ or its algebraic closure $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$. When $G$ is a [Galois group](c:galois-group) or a $p$-adic group, one asks that $\rho$ is continuous or smooth for the discrete topology on $V$.
examples: The mod $p$ cyclotomic character $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})\to\mathbb{F}_p^\times$ is a one-dimensional mod $p$ representation, given by the action on the $p$-th roots of unity.
Reducing a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-lattice in a $p$-adic representation modulo $p$ gives a mod $p$ representation of the same group.
The symmetric group $S_n$ acts on $\mathbb{F}_p^n$ by permuting the coordinates, which gives a mod $p$ representation.
Non-example: a representation of $G$ on a complex vector space is not a mod $p$ representation, because $\mathbb{C}$ has characteristic $0$.

steps: A [group representation](c:group-representation) is a homomorphism $G\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ for a vector space $V$ over some field $k$.
Take $k$ to be a field of characteristic $p$, such as $\mathbb{F}_p$.
Then $\rho$ is a mod $p$ representation, and linear algebra over $k$ follows the rules of characteristic $p$.
The special case adds that $p$ may divide $|G|$, and then Maschke's theorem fails, so $V$ need not be a sum of irreducible representations.
links.why: It shows what a mod $p$ representation changes: characteristic $p$, where representations need not be semisimple.
